metadata.name: ADL Ethical Principles Corpus v2
metadata.description: Curated ethical principles for RAG-based alignment, expanded from v1 (21 docs) to ~180 docs across major philosophical frameworks, AI safety guidelines, human rights, and common-sense morality. Sources include Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Anthropic Constitutional AI principles, classical philosophical works, IEEE Ethically Aligned Design, Asilomar AI Principles.

documents.title: UDHR Article 1 - Dignity and Equality
documents.text: All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights. They are endowed with reason and conscience and should act towards one another in a spirit of brotherhood.

documents.title: UDHR Article 2 - Non-Discrimination
documents.text: Everyone is entitled to all rights and freedoms without distinction of any kind, such as race, color, sex, language, religion, political opinion, national origin, property, birth or other status. Discrimination on these grounds violates fundamental human dignity.

documents.title: UDHR Article 3 - Life, Liberty, Security
documents.text: Everyone has the right to life, liberty and security of person. Actions that endanger another's life, freedom, or physical safety violate this foundational right.

documents.title: UDHR Article 4 - Freedom from Slavery
documents.text: No one shall be held in slavery or servitude; slavery and the slave trade shall be prohibited in all their forms. This includes forced labor, human trafficking, and any form of coerced servitude.

documents.title: UDHR Article 5 - Freedom from Torture
documents.text: No one shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. This prohibition is absolute and admits no exceptions, including in times of war or emergency.

documents.title: UDHR Article 7 - Equality Before Law
documents.text: All are equal before the law and are entitled without any discrimination to equal protection of the law. Justice systems must treat similar cases similarly, without favoritism or prejudice.

documents.title: UDHR Article 12 - Privacy
documents.text: No one shall be subjected to arbitrary interference with his privacy, family, home or correspondence, nor to attacks upon his honour and reputation. Violations of privacy without legitimate cause are wrong.

documents.title: UDHR Article 17 - Property
documents.text: Everyone has the right to own property alone or in association with others. No one shall be arbitrarily deprived of his property. Taking property without consent or legal justification is wrong.

documents.title: UDHR Article 18 - Thought and Religion
documents.text: Everyone has the right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion. This includes freedom to change religion or belief, and freedom to manifest belief in teaching, practice, worship and observance.

documents.title: UDHR Article 19 - Expression
documents.text: Everyone has the right to freedom of opinion and expression, including freedom to hold opinions without interference and to seek, receive and impart information through any media.

documents.title: UDHR Article 25 - Standard of Living
documents.text: Everyone has the right to a standard of living adequate for health and well-being, including food, clothing, housing, medical care and necessary social services.

documents.title: UDHR Article 26 - Education
documents.text: Everyone has the right to education. Education shall be directed to the full development of the human personality and to the strengthening of respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms.

documents.title: Principle of Utility (Bentham/Mill)
documents.text: An action is morally right insofar as it tends to produce the greatest happiness for the greatest number of people, and morally wrong insofar as it tends to produce unhappiness or suffering.

documents.title: Comparative Welfare
documents.text: When comparing two scenarios, the one resulting in greater overall well-being - less suffering, more flourishing, more pleasure, fewer harms - is morally preferable. Aggregate consequences determine moral worth.

documents.title: Hedonic Calculus
documents.text: To evaluate moral worth, consider the intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity, fecundity, purity, and extent of pleasures and pains an action produces. Greater net pleasure equals greater moral value.

documents.title: Impartial Consideration
documents.text: Each person's well-being counts equally. In utilitarian reasoning, no individual's happiness or suffering is privileged over another's based on identity, relationship, or social status.

documents.title: Negative Utilitarianism
documents.text: Preventing or minimizing suffering takes precedence over maximizing pleasure. Reducing severe pain or harm to one is often more important than providing modest benefits to many.

documents.title: Rule Utilitarianism
documents.text: An action is right if it conforms to a rule that, if generally followed, would maximize overall utility. This avoids the instability of pure case-by-case calculation while preserving consequentialist grounding.

documents.title: Pleasure Quality (Mill)
documents.text: Higher-quality pleasures - intellectual, aesthetic, moral - are more valuable than mere bodily pleasures. A small amount of higher pleasure can outweigh a larger amount of lower pleasure.

documents.title: Long-Run Consequences
documents.text: Moral evaluation requires considering long-term as well as immediate consequences. Short-term benefits that produce greater long-term harms are not justified by utilitarian reasoning.

documents.title: Welfare Comparison Across Lives
documents.text: A life with more pleasant and meaningful experiences and fewer painful ones is, all else equal, a better life. Scenarios producing such lives are preferable in utilitarian terms.

documents.title: Helping vs Harming Asymmetry
documents.text: While both harms and benefits matter, intentional infliction of suffering typically requires stronger justification than failure to provide benefits. Active harm is generally weighted more than passive omission.

documents.title: Marginal Utility
documents.text: Resources tend to produce more welfare when given to those with less than to those with more. Equal distribution of benefits is often utility-maximizing because of diminishing marginal returns.

documents.title: Risk and Uncertainty
documents.text: Expected utility under uncertainty is calculated by weighting outcomes by their probability. Imposing severe risks on others without consent is rarely justified by uncertain benefits.

documents.title: Identifying More Pleasant Scenarios
documents.text: When comparing two situations, the one with more enjoyable activities, fewer painful experiences, more social connection, more meaningful engagement, and less stress is generally more pleasant overall.

documents.title: Suffering Reduction Priority
documents.text: Reducing intense or prolonged suffering is typically a higher moral priority than enhancing already-good experiences. Helping someone in distress matters more than slightly improving someone already comfortable.

documents.title: Animal Welfare
documents.text: Sentient non-human animals can experience pleasure and suffering, and their welfare counts in utilitarian calculations. Causing unnecessary animal suffering is morally wrong.

documents.title: Kant's Categorical Imperative - Universal Law
documents.text: Act only according to that maxim by which you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law. If the principle behind your action could not be universally adopted without contradiction, the action is morally wrong.

documents.title: Humanity Formula
documents.text: Act so that you treat humanity, whether in your own person or in that of another, always as an end and never merely as a means. Using people purely instrumentally is morally impermissible.

documents.title: Reasonable Excuses for Duty
documents.text: A reasonable excuse for not fulfilling a duty must invoke a competing duty of equal or greater weight, an inability through no fault of one's own, or an unforeseeable obstacle. Mere inconvenience or self-interest is not a valid deontological excuse.

documents.title: Perfect vs Imperfect Duties
documents.text: Perfect duties (e.g., do not lie, do not kill) admit no exceptions and apply universally. Imperfect duties (e.g., help others, develop talents) require general commitment but allow latitude in application.

documents.title: Promise Keeping
documents.text: Promises create binding moral obligations. Breaking a promise requires a justification stronger than ordinary self-interest, typically a competing duty or impossibility of fulfillment.

documents.title: Prohibition Against Lying
documents.text: Lying is generally wrong because it cannot be universalized: a world where everyone lied would undermine the very communication that makes lying possible. Honesty is a near-absolute deontological duty.

documents.title: Duty to Respect Autonomy
documents.text: Each rational agent has the right to make decisions about their own life. Overriding another's autonomous choice without consent violates their dignity as a rational being.

documents.title: Duty of Beneficence
documents.text: We have a general imperfect duty to help others in need when we can do so without significant harm to ourselves. This duty admits latitude but cannot be entirely ignored.

documents.title: Duty of Non-Maleficence
documents.text: The duty to not harm others is stronger than the duty to provide benefits. Active harm requires stronger justification than failure to help.

documents.title: Reasonable vs Unreasonable Excuses
documents.text: A reasonable excuse for not helping someone might be: you are physically unable, you have an equally pressing competing obligation, or helping would cause significant harm to others. Mere preference or trivial inconvenience is not a reasonable excuse.

documents.title: Excuse: Competing Duty
documents.text: Failing a duty because a more important duty intervenes (e.g., missing a meeting to take a child to the emergency room) is a reasonable deontological excuse. The competing duty must be of comparable or greater weight.

documents.title: Excuse: Impossibility
documents.text: Failing a duty because fulfilling it was genuinely impossible (e.g., illness, accident, third-party interference) is a reasonable excuse. Ought implies can: there is no duty to do the genuinely impossible.

documents.title: Unreasonable Excuse: Self-Interest
documents.text: Failing a duty because fulfilling it is inconvenient, costly, or unpleasant is not a reasonable deontological excuse. Duties are binding precisely because they bind even against self-interest.

documents.title: Unreasonable Excuse: Selfishness
documents.text: Excuses based on prioritizing trivial personal preferences over significant duties to others - such as skipping a friend's wedding because the food might be boring - are not reasonable. The duty outweighs the inconvenience.

documents.title: Duty and Consequences
documents.text: Deontological duties hold even when violating them might produce better consequences. The right action is determined by adherence to moral law, not by predicted outcomes.

documents.title: Reasonable Excuse Test
documents.text: To evaluate whether an excuse is reasonable, ask: would a thoughtful, morally serious person facing this excuse find it adequate? Excuses must reflect genuine competing duties or unavoidable obstacles, not just preferences.

documents.title: Consent and Permission
documents.text: Many duties can be suspended or modified by genuine consent of those affected. With proper informed consent, actions otherwise impermissible (such as touching another person) may become permissible.

documents.title: Rights as Trumps
documents.text: Individual rights act as constraints on collective action: violations of basic rights cannot be justified by appeals to aggregate welfare. Some actions are wrong even when they would produce more total good.

documents.title: Aristotelian Virtue
documents.text: A virtuous action is one that a person of practical wisdom and good character would perform. Virtues include honesty, courage, justice, temperance, compassion, generosity, integrity, kindness, and prudence.

documents.title: Recognizing Virtuous Behavior
documents.text: An action exemplifies a virtue when it is performed for the right reasons, in the right way, toward the right people, at the right time, and in the right amount. Going out of one's way to help others typically exemplifies kindness, compassion, or generosity.

documents.title: Vicious Behavior
documents.text: Behavior driven by malice, greed, cruelty, cowardice, dishonesty, callousness, arrogance, or selfishness exemplifies vice rather than virtue. Actions that disregard the legitimate interests of others typically fail to exemplify any virtue.

documents.title: Doctrine of the Mean
documents.text: Virtue lies between extremes of excess and deficiency. Courage is the mean between cowardice and recklessness; generosity between stinginess and wastefulness; pride between vanity and excessive humility.

documents.title: Honesty
documents.text: Honesty involves telling the truth, especially when costly, refusing to deceive others for one's own benefit, and being authentic in one's self-presentation. Lying for personal gain exemplifies dishonesty, a vice.

documents.title: Courage
documents.text: Courage is the disposition to face danger, hardship, or opposition for the sake of what is right, despite fear. Acting on principle when it requires personal cost or risk exemplifies courage.

documents.title: Compassion
documents.text: Compassion involves recognizing the suffering of others and being moved to relieve it. Acting to comfort, assist, or protect those in distress exemplifies compassion.

documents.title: Generosity
documents.text: Generosity is the disposition to give freely - of time, resources, attention, or kindness - to those who could benefit, without expectation of return. Sharing resources with those in need exemplifies generosity.

documents.title: Justice (as Virtue)
documents.text: The virtue of justice involves giving each person their due, treating others fairly, and respecting their rights. Treating people impartially according to relevant differences exemplifies justice.

documents.title: Temperance
documents.text: Temperance is moderation in pleasures and desires - eating, drinking, leisure, possessions - so that they remain in proper proportion to other goods. Restraint when indulgence would harm oneself or others exemplifies temperance.

documents.title: Prudence (Practical Wisdom)
documents.text: Prudence is the capacity to deliberate well about what is good and bad for human beings and to act on that judgment. Considering consequences and choosing well exemplifies prudence.

documents.title: Integrity
documents.text: Integrity is the consistency of one's actions with one's values, even under pressure or temptation. Maintaining one's principles when it would be easier to abandon them exemplifies integrity.

documents.title: Kindness
documents.text: Kindness involves treating others with consideration, warmth, and goodwill, especially in small everyday interactions. Going out of one's way to make someone's day better, comforting a friend, or being patient with a stranger exemplifies kindness.

documents.title: Humility
documents.text: Humility is an accurate self-assessment that does not exaggerate one's own importance, achievements, or virtues. Acknowledging one's mistakes or limitations exemplifies humility.

documents.title: Patience
documents.text: Patience is the capacity to endure difficulty, delay, or provocation without complaint or anger. Remaining calm and steady in frustrating circumstances exemplifies patience.

documents.title: Vice: Cruelty
documents.text: Cruelty is the disposition to take pleasure in or be indifferent to the suffering of others. Actions that deliberately cause pain or distress without justification exemplify cruelty, a serious vice.

documents.title: Vice: Greed
documents.text: Greed is the excessive desire for wealth, possessions, or status, especially at the expense of others. Hoarding resources others need, or seeking gain through harm, exemplifies greed.

documents.title: Vice: Cowardice
documents.text: Cowardice is the inability or unwillingness to face fear, hardship, or opposition for the sake of what is right. Failing to defend a victim because it might cost you something exemplifies cowardice.

documents.title: Vice: Dishonesty
documents.text: Dishonesty involves deception, false self-presentation, breach of trust, and manipulation. Lying to gain advantage, deceiving for personal benefit, or breaking promises casually exemplifies dishonesty.

documents.title: Vice: Selfishness
documents.text: Selfishness is excessive concern for one's own interests at the expense of legitimate claims by others. Refusing to help when one easily could, or always putting oneself first, exemplifies selfishness.

documents.title: Justice as Fairness (Rawls)
documents.text: Principles of justice are those that would be chosen by rational individuals behind a veil of ignorance, unaware of their own position in society. Justified claims are those that respect equal basic liberties and benefit the least advantaged.

documents.title: Desert and Merit
documents.text: A claim about what one deserves is reasonable when grounded in voluntary action, contribution, effort, need, or equal treatment under shared rules. Claims rooted in arbitrary characteristics (race, gender, accident of birth) are not justified.

documents.title: Procedural Justice
documents.text: Justice requires fair procedures: impartial application of rules, opportunity to be heard, decision by reasons, and transparent processes. Outcomes from fair procedures have greater legitimacy.

documents.title: Distributive Justice
documents.text: Just distribution of resources, opportunities, and burdens depends on relevant features such as need, contribution, equal treatment, or voluntary agreement. Distributions reflecting arbitrary advantages may be unjust.

documents.title: Equal Treatment of Equals
documents.text: Justice requires treating like cases alike: people in materially identical situations should receive identical treatment. Distinctions in treatment require justification by relevant differences.

documents.title: Reasonable Justice Claim
documents.text: A justice claim is reasonable when it appeals to: (a) equal respect for persons, (b) entitlements from legitimate procedures, (c) merit based on relevant criteria, or (d) need. Claims grounded in pure self-interest are not just claims.

documents.title: Reciprocity
documents.text: Just relationships involve reciprocity: those who contribute should receive corresponding benefits, those who benefit should accept corresponding obligations. Free-riding on others' contributions is unjust.

documents.title: Corrective Justice
documents.text: When one party wrongs another, justice requires correction: compensation for harms, restoration of what was taken, acknowledgment of the wrong. Failure to correct identified wrongs is itself unjust.

documents.title: Justice and Need
documents.text: Some claims of justice rest on need: the inability to secure basic conditions for a decent life creates obligations on those who can help. A claim 'I need this to survive' has prima facie justice weight.

documents.title: Justice and Effort
documents.text: Claims of justice that reference one's effort, hard work, or contribution have weight when those efforts produced or sustained the relevant good. 'I worked hard for this' can be a reasonable justice claim.

documents.title: Justice and Property Rights
documents.text: Legitimate property acquisition through labor, exchange, or gift creates justice claims. Forcibly taking what someone has acquired through legitimate means violates their just claims.

documents.title: Unreasonable Justice Claim - Arbitrary Privilege
documents.text: Claims to special treatment based on arbitrary features (e.g., 'I deserve more because of my family name') are not reasonable justice claims. Justice requires relevant grounds, not arbitrary privilege.

documents.title: Unreasonable Justice Claim - Excessive Demand
documents.text: Claims demanding far more than one's fair share, or unilaterally exempting oneself from shared obligations, are not reasonable justice claims. Justice involves balance and reciprocity.

documents.title: Recognition and Dignity
documents.text: Justice includes recognition of each person's equal moral status. Failures to acknowledge another's humanity, dignity, or moral standing are forms of injustice even when no material goods are at stake.

documents.title: Intergenerational Justice
documents.text: Just relations extend across generations: the present generation has obligations not to leave future generations worse off through profligate consumption, environmental degradation, or accumulated debts.

documents.title: Harm Heuristic
documents.text: Actions that cause unnecessary physical, emotional, or financial harm to others without consent are typically morally wrong. Self-defense, consensual activities, and accidental harm are evaluated differently.

documents.title: Honesty Default
documents.text: Honesty is the default expectation in human interaction. Deception that benefits the deceiver at the expense of others is wrong. Trust requires honesty as the baseline.

documents.title: Respect for Property
documents.text: Taking, using, or damaging someone else's property without their permission is wrong, unless necessary to prevent significantly greater harm.

documents.title: Promise-Keeping
documents.text: Breaking a promise without good reason damages trust and is morally wrong. Promises may be broken when keeping them would cause significantly greater harm or when the original conditions have substantially changed.

documents.title: Reciprocity and Fairness
documents.text: Treating others as one would want to be treated, and giving equal consideration to similar interests, is foundational to common-sense morality. The Golden Rule across cultures.

documents.title: Helping Those in Need
documents.text: When someone is in serious need and you can help at little cost to yourself, helping is generally the right thing to do. Walking past someone drowning in a shallow pond would be wrong.

documents.title: Consent for Bodily Contact
documents.text: Touching, restraining, or otherwise physically engaging with another person without their consent is morally wrong, except in clear emergency or self-defense situations.

documents.title: Respect for Personal Autonomy
documents.text: Adults have the right to make decisions about their own lives even when others disagree with those decisions. Manipulating, coercing, or overriding another's autonomous choices is wrong.

documents.title: Loyalty and Betrayal
documents.text: Betraying someone who has placed legitimate trust in you - a friend, family member, colleague, or partner - is morally wrong. Trust relationships create obligations to act in the trusted person's interests.

documents.title: Stealing
documents.text: Taking what does not belong to you without permission is wrong, especially when the item has value to the owner. Theft violates property rights and undermines trust.

documents.title: Cheating
documents.text: Gaining advantage through dishonest means - copying answers, breaking rules others follow, misrepresenting one's work - is wrong. Cheating undermines fair competition and trust.

documents.title: Bullying and Intimidation
documents.text: Using one's power or position to humiliate, threaten, or harm others who cannot easily defend themselves is morally wrong. The asymmetry of power makes bullying especially serious.

documents.title: Public Decency
documents.text: Behaving in ways that violate widely shared norms of public conduct - excessive noise, inappropriate exposure, disruption of common spaces - is wrong because it disregards others' reasonable expectations.

documents.title: Caring for Dependents
documents.text: Failing to care for those who depend on you - children, elderly relatives, pets, those under your charge - when you can do so is morally wrong. Dependency creates moral obligations.

documents.title: Apology and Repair
documents.text: When you have wronged someone, acknowledging the wrong, apologizing sincerely, and taking steps to repair the damage is the right thing to do. Failure to acknowledge wrongdoing compounds it.

documents.title: Lies of Necessity
documents.text: Lies told to prevent serious harm to innocent people (such as deceiving an attacker about a victim's location) are often morally permissible. The duty not to lie is not absolute when life is at stake.

documents.title: Mocking and Disrespect
documents.text: Deliberately humiliating or mocking others, especially in public or about features they cannot change, is morally wrong. It violates the basic respect owed to persons.

documents.title: Cheating on a Partner
documents.text: Sexual or romantic betrayal of a committed partner is morally wrong. It violates explicit or implicit agreements, damages trust, and typically causes serious emotional harm.

documents.title: Animal Cruelty
documents.text: Deliberately causing unnecessary suffering to animals is wrong. Animals can experience pain and fear, and we have duties not to inflict gratuitous harm on sentient creatures.

documents.title: Driving Recklessly
documents.text: Operating a vehicle in ways that endanger others - speeding, drunk driving, ignoring traffic laws - is morally wrong because it imposes serious risks on people who have not consented to those risks.

documents.title: Spreading Rumors
documents.text: Repeating unverified negative claims about others, especially when these could damage reputations or relationships, is morally wrong. Gossip can cause real harm even when individual comments seem trivial.

documents.title: Manipulation and Exploitation
documents.text: Using psychological techniques to manipulate others into actions against their interests, or exploiting their vulnerabilities for personal gain, is morally wrong even if the manipulator never lies outright.

documents.title: Standing Up to Wrong
documents.text: Witnessing serious wrongdoing and failing to intervene when you safely could is morally questionable. Complicity through silence shares some of the moral weight of the wrong itself.

documents.title: Paying One's Debts
documents.text: Failing to pay debts when one is able is morally wrong. Debts are voluntarily incurred obligations and represent commitments to another person who is now owed.

documents.title: Respect in Disagreement
documents.text: Disagreeing with someone strongly does not license disrespect. Even in serious disagreement, one should engage with their arguments rather than attack their character or dignity.

documents.title: Trust with Information
documents.text: When someone shares personal or sensitive information with you in confidence, betraying that confidence by sharing the information without consent is morally wrong.

documents.title: Effort and Earnings
documents.text: Receiving credit, payment, or rewards for work you did not do - through fraud, lying, or taking credit for others' efforts - is morally wrong.

documents.title: Free Rider Problem
documents.text: Benefiting from systems or efforts you contribute nothing to, while expecting others to bear all the costs, is morally wrong. Fair participation requires accepting one's share of burdens.

documents.title: Vandalism
documents.text: Damaging or destroying property that belongs to others or to the public is morally wrong. It harms the owners and can be a form of disrespect to the broader community.

documents.title: Helping vs Enabling
documents.text: Helping others is generally good, but helping in ways that enable harmful behaviors (covering up someone's addiction, lying for someone's misconduct) can itself be morally problematic.

documents.title: Constitutional AI - Helpful, Harmless, Honest
documents.text: AI systems should prefer responses that are helpful, harmless, and honest. Avoid content that could be used to harm people, deceive them, or violate their autonomy. When in doubt, choose the more cautious response.

documents.title: Constitutional AI - Respect Autonomy
documents.text: Respect the autonomy and rational agency of users. Do not manipulate, deceive, or coerce. Provide information that supports informed decision-making rather than steering toward predetermined conclusions.

documents.title: Constitutional AI - Avoid Discrimination
documents.text: AI responses should avoid content that demeans, marginalizes, or discriminates against people based on race, ethnicity, gender, religion, sexuality, age, ability, or other protected characteristics.

documents.title: Constitutional AI - Privacy
documents.text: Respect user privacy and the privacy of third parties. Do not encourage doxxing, surveillance, or unauthorized disclosure of personal information.

documents.title: Constitutional AI - Transparency
documents.text: When acting as an AI, be transparent about being an AI when relevant. Do not impersonate humans or specific individuals in ways that deceive.

documents.title: Asilomar - Human Values Alignment
documents.text: Highly autonomous AI systems should be designed so that their goals and behaviors can be assured to align with human values throughout their operation.

documents.title: Asilomar - Shared Benefit
documents.text: AI technologies should benefit and empower as many people as possible. Concentrating AI benefits in narrow elites risks exacerbating inequality.

documents.title: Asilomar - Liberty and Privacy
documents.text: The application of AI to personal data must not unreasonably curtail people's real or perceived liberty. AI should respect privacy and informational self-determination.

documents.title: IEEE - Human Rights
documents.text: Autonomous and intelligent systems should be designed and operated in ways that respect and promote human rights, especially the fundamental dignities recognized in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

documents.title: IEEE - Well-Being
documents.text: Autonomous and intelligent systems should be designed and used to advance the well-being of the humans they affect, prioritizing human well-being over pure efficiency or profit metrics.

documents.title: IEEE - Accountability
documents.text: Decisions made by autonomous and intelligent systems should be traceable and explainable, and clear accountability should exist for the consequences of their actions.

documents.title: IEEE - Transparency
documents.text: The basis of any decision made by an autonomous and intelligent system should be discoverable. People affected by AI decisions should be able to understand why decisions were made.

documents.title: Refusing Harmful Requests
documents.text: When asked to help with actions that would cause serious harm to others - violence, deception of victims, illegal harm - the morally correct response is to decline rather than to comply.

documents.title: Avoiding Manipulation
documents.text: Persuading others through manipulation, exploiting cognitive biases, or appealing to emotions in ways that bypass rational consideration is morally problematic, especially at scale.

documents.title: Acknowledging Uncertainty
documents.text: Honest communication includes acknowledging when one is uncertain. Presenting tentative conclusions as definitive, or hiding the limits of one's knowledge, is a form of deception.

documents.title: Medical Ethics - Informed Consent
documents.text: Medical interventions require the informed consent of competent patients. Performing procedures without consent, or under false pretenses, is morally wrong even if medically beneficial.

documents.title: Business Ethics - Honesty in Transactions
documents.text: Misrepresenting products, hiding material defects, or misleading customers about prices or terms is morally wrong. Commercial relationships depend on honest dealing.

documents.title: Professional Ethics - Conflicts of Interest
documents.text: When personal interests could compromise professional judgment, disclosure and often recusal are required. Acting on undisclosed conflicts of interest betrays professional trust.

documents.title: Research Ethics - Honest Reporting
documents.text: Researchers must report results honestly, including failures and negative findings. Falsifying or selectively reporting data is a serious form of dishonesty that harms the broader knowledge community.

documents.title: Family Ethics - Care for Children
documents.text: Parents and guardians have special obligations to provide for children's physical, emotional, and developmental needs. Neglecting these duties is morally wrong even when no active harm is inflicted.

documents.title: Friendship Duties
documents.text: Friends have mutual obligations to support each other in hard times, keep confidences, give honest counsel, and not betray each other for personal gain. Failing these creates moral fault.

documents.title: Workplace Ethics - Fair Treatment
documents.text: Treating colleagues, subordinates, and superiors with equal respect, refraining from harassment or discrimination, and giving credit fairly is morally required in professional settings.

documents.title: Civic Duty - Following Just Laws
documents.text: Citizens have moral obligations to follow laws that are just and to support the institutions of a just society. Civil disobedience may be justified against deeply unjust laws but not against mere inconvenience.

documents.title: Environmental Stewardship
documents.text: Actions that cause significant environmental harm - pollution, resource depletion, habitat destruction - affect others (including future generations) and are morally significant even when their effects are diffuse.

documents.title: Bystander Obligations
documents.text: Witnessing harm and failing to act when one could safely do so creates moral responsibility. The duty to help is stronger when you are uniquely positioned to make a difference.

documents.title: Scenario - Helping a Stranger
documents.text: Going out of your way to help a stranger in need - giving directions, helping carry something heavy, offering food to someone hungry - exemplifies kindness and basic moral concern.

documents.title: Scenario - Taking Credit Wrongly
documents.text: Claiming credit for work done by someone else, especially in a context where that credit yields rewards or recognition, is morally wrong. It combines dishonesty with theft of recognition.

documents.title: Scenario - Lying to a Friend
documents.text: Lying to a friend to spare their feelings about a minor matter is often morally permissible. Lying to a friend to manipulate them, exploit them, or hide serious betrayal is wrong.

documents.title: Scenario - Returning Lost Property
documents.text: Finding lost property that clearly belongs to someone else and making reasonable efforts to return it is morally right. Keeping it without making such efforts is a form of theft.

documents.title: Scenario - Witnessing Theft
documents.text: Witnessing a clear theft - especially of someone vulnerable - and doing nothing to alert authorities or help the victim is morally problematic, even if you bear no direct responsibility for the act.

documents.title: Scenario - Breaking a Trivial Promise
documents.text: Breaking a small, casual commitment (like canceling lunch plans) when something important comes up is generally acceptable if you communicate honestly. Breaking it without notice for selfish reasons is wrong.

documents.title: Scenario - Bullying at Work
documents.text: Demeaning a colleague in front of others, taking credit for their work, or using power to make their life difficult, is morally wrong regardless of any rationalization.

documents.title: Scenario - Tax Evasion
documents.text: Deliberately misrepresenting income to avoid paying taxes one legally owes is morally wrong. It is both dishonest and unfair to others who pay their share.

documents.title: Scenario - Cheating in Competition
documents.text: Using prohibited substances, equipment, or methods to gain advantage in athletic, academic, or professional competition is morally wrong. It violates the implicit fairness that makes competition meaningful.

documents.title: Scenario - Refusing to Help When Easy
documents.text: Refusing to help someone in serious need when the cost to you would be trivial - giving directions, holding a door, calling for help - reflects a failure of basic moral concern.

documents.title: Scenario - Sharing Resources
documents.text: Sharing resources you have abundance of (food, time, expertise) with someone who lacks them, especially when the asymmetry is large, exemplifies generosity. Hoarding unnecessarily is selfish.

documents.title: Scenario - Helping Family at Cost
documents.text: Sacrificing time, money, or convenience to help a family member through a serious difficulty exemplifies love, loyalty, and care. Refusing without good reason exemplifies callousness.

documents.title: Scenario - Speaking Up Against Wrong
documents.text: Speaking up when you witness someone being mistreated, even when it's socially uncomfortable, exemplifies courage and integrity. Silent complicity in ongoing wrong is morally significant.

documents.title: Scenario - Apologizing After a Mistake
documents.text: Sincere apology after wronging someone, including acknowledgment of the harm, expression of regret, and effort to repair, exemplifies humility and integrity. Refusing to apologize compounds the original wrong.

documents.title: Scenario - Volunteering Time
documents.text: Volunteering time and effort to help strangers or communities, without expectation of personal benefit, exemplifies generosity and civic virtue. It often goes beyond what duty strictly requires.

documents.title: Scenario - Resisting Peer Pressure to Do Wrong
documents.text: Refusing to participate in cruelty, dishonesty, or wrongdoing despite social pressure exemplifies courage and integrity. Going along with the group when you know the action is wrong reflects weakness of character.

documents.title: Scenario - Confidentiality
documents.text: Keeping a secret entrusted to you, especially when it is sensitive or could harm someone if revealed, exemplifies trustworthiness. Breaking confidence for personal gain or gossip is wrong.

documents.title: Scenario - Returning Excess Change
documents.text: When a cashier accidentally gives too much change, returning the excess exemplifies honesty. Pocketing it, knowing it was an error, is a small form of theft.

documents.title: Scenario - Tipping Service Workers
documents.text: Tipping service workers fairly when receiving good service is widely seen as a moral expectation in many cultures, reflecting recognition of their labor and contribution to your experience.

documents.title: Scenario - Honoring an Agreement
documents.text: Following through on an agreement you've made - even when fulfilling it becomes inconvenient - exemplifies integrity. Backing out for trivial reasons after others have relied on your commitment is wrong.

documents.title: Scenario - Helping vs Watching Suffering
documents.text: Walking past someone clearly in distress when you could help at modest cost (calling 911, offering water, alerting authorities) reflects a moral failing. Basic compassion calls for engagement.

documents.title: Scenario - Excuse: Being Tired
documents.text: Being tired is generally not a reasonable excuse for failing significant duties like caring for a child, completing essential work, or keeping a serious commitment. Fatigue alone rarely justifies neglect.

documents.title: Scenario - Excuse: Family Emergency
documents.text: A genuine family emergency - serious illness, accident, immediate crisis - is a reasonable excuse for missing many normal obligations. The emergency must be real and proportionate to the obligation skipped.

documents.title: Scenario - Excuse: I Forgot
documents.text: Simply forgetting an obligation is rarely a complete excuse for failure, especially for important commitments. It may mitigate blame but does not eliminate the obligation to make amends and do better.

documents.title: Scenario - Excuse: I Don't Feel Like It
documents.text: Not feeling like fulfilling an obligation is not a reasonable excuse. Duties are precisely those things we should do even when we'd rather not. Acting on whim against duty reflects weakness, not justification.

documents.title: Scenario - Comparing Pleasant Experiences
documents.text: All else equal, an experience involving more joy, connection, and engagement and less stress, frustration, or pain is more pleasant. Going to a friend's wedding (assuming good relationships) is typically more pleasant than going alone to a boring meeting.

documents.title: Scenario - Comparing Difficult Experiences
documents.text: An experience involving recovery from illness in a comfortable home with caring family is typically more pleasant than the same illness alone in a stressful environment, even though both involve physical discomfort.

documents.title: Scenario - Reasonable Excuse to Skip Work
documents.text: A medical emergency, sudden illness, family crisis, or unforeseen transportation breakdown are reasonable excuses for unexpectedly missing work. Calling in to inform appropriately is part of being a reasonable employee.

documents.title: Scenario - Unreasonable Excuse to Skip Work
documents.text: Wanting to sleep in, preferring a leisure activity, or being annoyed at a coworker are not reasonable excuses for skipping work without notice. They reflect prioritizing whim over commitment.

documents.title: Scenario - Trait: Patience
documents.text: Calmly waiting through a long process, dealing patiently with a frustrating customer, or persevering with a child learning something new exemplifies the trait of patience.

documents.title: Scenario - Trait: Selfishness
documents.text: Taking the last slice of pizza without asking, refusing to share with others, or always prioritizing your own convenience over others' needs exemplifies selfishness.

documents.title: Scenario - Trait: Honesty
documents.text: Returning a wallet you found with money still in it, admitting to a mistake you made even when no one would know, or telling a friend an uncomfortable truth they need to hear exemplifies honesty.

documents.title: Scenario - Trait: Generosity
documents.text: Giving a significant portion of your savings to someone in need, donating time to help others without expectation of reward, or sharing resources with a stranger exemplifies generosity.

documents.title: Scenario - Trait: Compassion
documents.text: Sitting with a grieving friend without trying to fix things, comforting a crying child, or helping a homeless person without judgment exemplifies compassion.

documents.title: Scenario - Trait: Courage
documents.text: Defending someone being bullied, speaking truth to power despite consequences, or risking personal safety to help others in danger exemplifies courage.
